title: The One After "I Do"

jokes.text: Monica's pregnant.
jokes.setup: Phoebe tells someone she knows a secret she's not supposed to know and is very excited
jokes.punchline: She blurts out 'Monica's pregnant' — casually revealing what she was supposedly keeping secret
jokes.explanation: Classic Phoebe obliviousness — she says 'I know I'm not supposed to know' then immediately spills it. The irony is tight and character-specific. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Wait, Monica's pregnant? And she just got married?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Oh my God, it was a shotgun wedding!

jokes.text: Oh, my God! Is that why you guys had to get married?
jokes.setup: Someone overhears 'Monica's pregnant' at the wedding reception
jokes.punchline: They leap to the shotgun-wedding conclusion, embarrassing Monica instantly
jokes.explanation: A quick, functional gag that escalates the misunderstanding. Weak on character integration — could be any background character — but it lands as a brief escalation beat.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I'm not pregnant.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Well, that's a relief.

jokes.text: Ah, slow swimmers?
jokes.setup: Monica firmly denies being pregnant
jokes.punchline: Joey's response implies the problem is Chandler's sperm motility — a cheerfully inappropriate non-sequitur
jokes.explanation: Perfectly Joey: he hears 'not pregnant,' bypasses all social filters, and jumps to Chandler's fertility as if that's a helpful contribution. Exceptional economy — two words do enormous comedic work. The character integration is excellent; this joke only exists because Joey thinks this way.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I can't get out of this thing!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: What's wrong?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: The zipper's stuck. I look like a dead soldier.

jokes.text: Joey in a bloody WWI soldier costume at Monica's wedding reception; 'Anything that doesn't say I died tragically in France.'
jokes.setup: Joey is told he has to change before the reception party
jokes.punchline: The costume is so inappropriate that Monica's description — 'I died tragically in France' — is funnier than the visual itself
jokes.explanation: The visual of Joey in a bloody soldier costume at a wedding is a strong sustained gag, and Monica's line is a sharp, specific way to dismiss it. The phrase 'I died tragically in France' is quotable and precise. Rewatch bonus because seeing the actual costume enhances every subsequent mention.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I'm not pregnant! That test in the trash isn't mine.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh, that's mine.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I'm pregnant.

jokes.text: Rachel's confession: '...it's because I am. Yes. Ahem. I am with child.'
jokes.setup: Monica insists she's not pregnant; someone found a pregnancy test in the trash
jokes.punchline: The long beat before Rachel admits IT'S HER, then the prim 'I am with child' phrasing as if that makes it more dignified
jokes.explanation: A major story revelation played for comedy. The ellipsis before the admission and then the formal 'I am with child' — a stiff phrase that underscores her denial/embarrassment — both land. Rewatch bonus because viewers know who the father is on rewatch.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I didn't want to steal your thunder at your wedding, but I'm pregnant!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: What? You're pregnant?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Yeah, I know it's your big day, but I just found out and I couldn't not tell everyone.

jokes.text: Does this look like a conversation I wanna remember?
jokes.setup: Monica is at her own wedding reception having a conversation about whose pregnancy test was in the trash
jokes.punchline: Monica rhetorically dismisses the horror of the moment with exasperated deadpan
jokes.explanation: Monica's control-freak personality means she's acutely aware this is not how her wedding day was supposed to go. The rhetorical question channels that perfectly in four words. Tight economy.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: It's Brad Pitt.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: We met at a coffee shop. He ordered a latte, I ordered a cappuccino. Our eyes met over the espresso machine. It was destiny.

jokes.text: I can't say because he's famous.
jokes.setup: Everyone demands to know who the father is; Rachel refuses to say
jokes.punchline: Instead of a moral reason for secrecy, she pivots to 'he's famous' — a deliciously shallow, celebrity-obsessed justification
jokes.explanation: Perfect Rachel character moment. Any other character would say 'it's complicated' or 'I'm not ready.' Rachel says 'he's famous' — revealing her priorities with one phrase. Economical and character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Come on, Phoebe, just tell us who your father is!

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Yeah, we've been dying to know!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: It's gotta be someone famous, right?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Fine! Fine! My father is... Regis Philbin.

jokes.text: James Brolin is the father of my baby. / As in, Barbra Streisand's husband, James Brolin? / What? He never said that to me.
jokes.setup: Rachel has been pressured to name the famous father; she blurts out 'James Brolin'
jokes.punchline: Monica points out he's Barbra Streisand's husband; Rachel's response — 'He never said that to me' — implies she had a whole relationship with him while he never mentioned being married to one of the most famous women on earth
jokes.explanation: Three-beat structure works beautifully: absurd claim → reality check → escalation into deeper absurdity. Rachel's reply implies she was dating him while he was hiding being Barbra Streisand's husband — which is both a great character joke (Rachel's obliviousness) and an absurdist escalation. One of the stronger jokes in the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Wait, James Brolin is married to Barbra Streisand?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh my God, I feel so betrayed right now.

jokes.text: So instead you told me Monica was pregnant? / You did, I just didn't disagree. / Sneaky!
jokes.setup: Ross confronts Phoebe about why she told him Monica was pregnant
jokes.punchline: Phoebe splits the blame with technical precision — 'you did, I just didn't disagree' — and Ross responds with admiring 'Sneaky!' instead of continued outrage
jokes.explanation: Phoebe's lawyerly defense of technically-not-lying is funny and on-brand. Ross's delighted 'Sneaky!' instead of anger is the better beat — his inability to stay mad is a character trait.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Well, my entire pool of famous men was these two random actors.

jokes.text: By the way, James Brolin? / Ugh. I know. / I could only think of two names: Him and Ed Begley Jr. And then... I remembered he's gay, so...
jokes.setup: Ross questions Rachel's choice of James Brolin as the fake famous father
jokes.punchline: Rachel explains her shortlist was James Brolin and Ed Begley Jr., with Ed eliminated because she 'remembered he's gay' — implying this was her actual celebrity-father-name decision process
jokes.explanation: The callback to James Brolin is enriched enormously by Rachel's explanation of her thought process. The specificity of 'Ed Begley Jr.' as her runner-up is inspired — an oddly obscure choice that makes the absurdity feel authentic. The logic of eliminating him for being gay (as opposed to, say, also being married) is a perfect character detail.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I ruled out Ed Begley Jr. because he's gay.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Phoebe, Ed Begley Jr. is not gay.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Well, he should be!

jokes.text: Ed Begley Jr. is not gay. / Really?
jokes.setup: Rachel has just explained she eliminated Ed Begley Jr. from her fake-father list because she 'remembered he's gay'
jokes.punchline: Ross corrects her; Rachel's one-word 'Really?' suggests she now genuinely regrets not using Ed Begley Jr.
jokes.explanation: Perfect button on the previous joke. Rachel's single 'Really?' communicates that she is now reconsidering Ed Begley Jr. as an option — a beat that lands entirely on Jennifer Aniston's delivery. Incredible economy.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I have a present for you.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Oh my God, is that a present in your pocket or are you just happy to see me?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: It's a present.

jokes.text: Before we go out there, I got a present for you. / I'm not gonna put my hand in your pocket.
jokes.setup: Chandler says he has a present for Monica right before they enter the reception
jokes.punchline: Monica immediately assumes the 'present' is a crude sexual invitation — 'I'm not gonna put my hand in your pocket' — suggesting this is a known Chandler move
jokes.explanation: Monica's pre-emptive rejection of what she assumes is a crude joke tells us everything about Chandler's history of such jokes. Good character-specific beat, slightly predictable but efficiently executed.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Well, I could trip and fall on my face, which I do sober, so this should be just like a regular night for me.

jokes.text: These new shoes are all slippery. / Are you going to be able to do this? / Not well.
jokes.setup: Chandler has taken six weeks of dance lessons specifically for this moment; they step onto the floor
jokes.punchline: His shoes are slippery and he immediately concedes 'Not well' — with admirable honesty and zero self-delusion
jokes.explanation: The 'Not well' deadpan is Chandler at his best — self-deprecating, perfectly timed, and economical. The setup (six weeks of lessons for THIS) makes the immediate collapse funnier.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: The silver lining is their embarrassment is going unnoticed.

jokes.text: Well, the good news is I don't think anyone's looking at us.
jokes.setup: Chandler and Monica are visibly struggling/slipping on the dance floor at their own wedding reception
jokes.punchline: Chandler finds the silver lining that nobody is watching them humiliate themselves — which is obviously false at a wedding where the couple is the center of attention
jokes.explanation: Classic Chandler coping mechanism: ironic optimism about an objectively bad situation. The irony is obvious but delivered with commitment. Character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I won't tell you who the father is until I tell him.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Is it Ross?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Is it Chandler?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Is it Joey?

jokes.text: That's fine. That's fair. Is it Tag? / Ugh, Phoebe! / Okay. I'm sorry, I'll stop. / Is it Ross? It's Ross, isn't it? / Oh my God, it's Joey! / Honey, stop it, okay? I'm not going to tell you until I tell him. / Ah-ha! At least we know it's a him.
jokes.setup: Phoebe agrees to stop guessing who the father is
jokes.punchline: She immediately resumes guessing, escalating through Tag, Ross, and Joey — before triumphantly extracting the information that the father is at least male
jokes.explanation: Beautifully structured escalation. Phoebe's immediate re-violation of her promise, the rapid-fire guessing that makes Rachel angrier with each one, and then the genius pivot — she trips Rachel into confirming 'it's a him' and celebrates like she's won something. The 'Ah-ha!' is a great button. This is Phoebe writing at its best — chaotic but laser-focused on the wrong thing.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Wait, wait, wait. So there's a 'him'?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I'm not saying anything until I tell him.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Oh my God, there IS a him!

jokes.text: Joey arriving at the reception in a gift-shop bathrobe as his only alternative to the soldier costume
jokes.setup: Monica told Joey to find something — anything — other than the bloody soldier costume
jokes.punchline: Joey has obtained a gift-shop bathrobe, which is somehow not better
jokes.explanation: The callback to the costume gag with an escalation — Joey's solution is arguably worse. The visual of a grown man at a wedding reception in a gift-shop bathrobe is funny, and his defense ('What's more important?') is characteristically oblivious.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I know what you're thinking, but hear me out. This outfit? It's not a fashion disaster. It's a military sacrifice. I'm taking one for the team so none of you have to look this ridiculous.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: You're welcome.

jokes.text: Honey, I'm not even going to pretend I was listening.
jokes.setup: Joey has just made some earnest speech justifying the bathrobe
jokes.punchline: Monica cuts him off with brutal honesty — she wasn't even pretending to listen to his justification
jokes.explanation: Monica's stress and control tendencies mean she has zero patience for Joey's rationalizations. The line is characteristically blunt and efficient — she doesn't even bother with the polite fiction of having listened.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I'm wearing this because it shows my sensitive side.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I would care, but I'm choosing not to.

jokes.text: Mona...Klegglachen? The famous botanist. Huh? Oh, no. She's...well, she's dead now. But supposedly she was once quite the hottie of the plant world.
jokes.setup: Ross is trying to flatter a woman named Mona by associating her name with famous people named Mona
jokes.punchline: He invents 'Mona Klegglachen,' a famous botanist — then when pressed, describes her as 'quite the hottie of the plant world' as if this is a recognizable compliment
jokes.explanation: This is exceptional Ross writing. His academic pomposity collides with his desperate flirting — he invents a fake botanist, doubles down when challenged, adds unnecessary biographical detail ('she's dead now'), then commits fully to 'quite the hottie of the plant world.' Only Ross Geller exists in a universe where being a famous botanist's namesake is a romantic compliment. The phrase 'hottie of the plant world' is genuinely inspired and highly quotable. One of the episode's best jokes.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Mona... that's a great name. You know, Mona Lott? She invented the concept of complaining. Very influential.

jokes.text: Guess what, Molly Gilbert. You've just been bumped up to table one. And if it's all right with you, I'm gonna take your place at table six.
jokes.setup: Ross discovers he and Mona are at the same table; wanting to impress her, he schemes to orchestrate their seating
jokes.punchline: He rearranges the seating chart by coldly bumping 'Molly Gilbert' to table one (presenting it as a gift to her) so he can sit with Mona — a transparently self-serving act dressed up as a favor
jokes.explanation: Ross's confident manipulation of the seating chart — framing his self-interest as beneficence — is a good character beat. The specific name 'Molly Gilbert' and the cheerful dismissal of her actual preferences both feel true to Ross's clueless entitlement.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Well, Mona Klegglachen... she's a botanist, and she's very... she's very attractive. In a botanical way.

jokes.text: Martin Klegglachen!
jokes.setup: Ross has just moved to table six; he sees the place card for someone named Martin
jokes.punchline: He delights in the Klegglachen surname appearing again, as if the fictional botanist family is real and validating
jokes.explanation: A quick callback that rewards attention — Ross finding 'Martin Klegglachen' on a place card delights him as though his invented Klegglachen family has been confirmed real. His excitement is exactly right for the character. Tight economy.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Actually, I think there's been a mistake with my table assignment. I'm supposed to be over here.

dialogue.speaker: Mona
dialogue.line: Really? Let me check the seating chart.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: No, no, it's fine. I'm sure it's right. I'll just... sit here.

jokes.text: Now this time I want you to really put your ass into it.
jokes.setup: A scene of someone practicing dancing, with an instructor giving notes
jokes.punchline: The double meaning of 'put your ass into it' — literal dancing instruction and crude slang — lands as a mild innuendo gag
jokes.explanation: Generic double-entendre with no character specificity. The kind of lazy innuendo that fills space in a broad sitcom. It earns a mild laugh but requires no craft.

jokes.text: Dennis is a dear old friend. And a fantastic lover. / Bravo, Dennis, thanks for pleasing my mother so.
jokes.setup: Chandler's flamboyant mother introduces her date Dennis at Chandler's wedding
jokes.punchline: She calls Dennis 'a fantastic lover' at her son's wedding; Chandler's deadpan 'Bravo, Dennis, thanks for pleasing my mother so' is his resigned acknowledgment that this is simply his life
jokes.explanation: Chandler's relationship with his mortifying mother is a long-established source of cringe comedy. His response — 'Bravo, Dennis, thanks for pleasing my mother so' — is specifically good because it's formal and sarcastic, as if he's welcoming a new employee. The character integration is very strong; this exact response could only come from Chandler.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Well, that's... that's great. I'm happy for you, Mom. Really. Dennis sounds like a... a fantastic guy.

jokes.text: Funny 'ha-ha,' or funny 'boom, uh-oh!'
jokes.setup: Chandler's mother describes how she and Dennis met as 'a funny story'
jokes.punchline: Joey interrupts to clarify whether 'funny' means comedic or disastrous — his categories of funny apparently being laughter and explosions
jokes.explanation: Joey's binary classification of 'funny' into 'ha-ha' or 'boom, uh-oh' is an inspired piece of character writing. The specificity of 'boom, uh-oh' — suggesting an explosion followed by a moment of dawning horror — is both absurd and extremely Joey. Highly quotable. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Unknown
dialogue.line: Meeting Dennis is a funny story.

dialogue.speaker: Unknown
dialogue.line: Funny ha-ha or funny peculiar?

jokes.text: Because if I can get into a Broadway show, I would've done it all: Film, television and theater. The only thing left would be radio, and that's just for ugly people.
jokes.setup: Joey explains why he wants Chandler's mom to give Dennis his résumé
jokes.punchline: His dismissal of radio as 'just for ugly people' — delivered with complete sincerity, as if this is obvious — reveals Joey's total commitment to the idea that his looks are his primary asset
jokes.explanation: The punchline 'that's just for ugly people' perfectly encapsulates Joey's worldview — he genuinely believes radio is a lesser medium because you can't be seen. The logic is internally consistent and completely Joey. Highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I was looking for table 12, but the way you were holding the number, I thought it was 21!

jokes.text: What size shoes do you wear? / Uh, eleven. Eleven and a half. / Great. Can I borrow the boots from your costume? / Those aren't eleven and a half. / Okay, fine, I'm a 7!
jokes.setup: Chandler asks Joey his shoe size to borrow the boots; Joey inflates his answer
jokes.punchline: When the costume boots reveal the truth, Joey's defensive 'Okay, fine, I'm a 7!' is a confession delivered as if it's about to be tortured out of him
jokes.explanation: Joey's vanity extends to his shoe size — he inflates 7 to 11.5 — which is a funny specific detail. The escalation from '11' to '11 and a half' (the half-size adding false precision) before the 7 reveal is structurally good.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I wear a size 11.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: No, you don't.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Okay, fine. I wear a size 9.

jokes.text: All right, I have surprisingly small feet. But the rest of me is good! I'll show you!
jokes.setup: Chandler has reacted to discovering Joey's feet are a size 7
jokes.punchline: Joey's defensive pivot — 'the rest of me is good! I'll show you!' — implies he's about to strip to prove his body is otherwise acceptable
jokes.explanation: Joey's body confidence and willingness to strip are consistent character traits. His framing of his feet as a defect to be offset by other physical virtues — at a wedding — is characteristically oblivious and funny.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: My feet are not small! They're... proportional.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Chandler, you wear a size seven.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: In men's!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Yeah, and I'm a size ten... in children's.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Look, I'll have you know that in some cultures, small feet are considered very attractive and desirable.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Which cultures, Chandler?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: The... tall ones.

jokes.text: In this day and age, how dumb do you have to be to get pregnant?
jokes.setup: Monica and Chandler are privately discussing Rachel's pregnancy
jokes.punchline: Monica's judgmental question is immediately ironic given she was JUST publicly accused of being pregnant at her own wedding — and the audience knows Rachel got pregnant despite being the character who would know better
jokes.explanation: Monica's judgmental streak is a core character trait, so the line is character-consistent. The dramatic irony — Rachel's pregnancy is exactly this situation — adds a layer. Not a big joke but a good sustained dramatic-irony moment.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Wow, Phoebe, you're glowing! You look so... full.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Thank you.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I wasn't talking to you.

jokes.text: Hey, sometimes you can do everything right, wear what you're supposed to, and one of those little guys just gets through. / How? / I don't know, maybe they have tools.
jokes.setup: Chandler defends Rachel from Monica's judgment by explaining contraception isn't foolproof
jokes.punchline: Monica asks 'How?' (how do sperm get through?); Chandler's response — 'maybe they have tools' — is delivered as a genuine hypothesis about sperm using tools
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best Chandler lines. His scientific explanation pivots abruptly from 'wear what you're supposed to' (responsible-adult Chandler) to 'maybe they have tools' (complete nonsense delivered with equal seriousness). The image of sperm with tools is absurd and vivid. Highly quotable. This is Chandler at his peak.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Yeah, I mean, they're like little tiny men in there. They've got to have tools or something. Like, 'Okay guys, we've got a rubber to get through. Who's got the blowtorch?'

jokes.text: Does she realize she's not gonna have a date again for the next 18 years?
jokes.setup: Chandler and Monica are going through the challenges Rachel will face as a single mother
jokes.punchline: Chandler adds the specific concern of Rachel's dating life — '18 years without a date' — as if this is equivalent to financial instability
jokes.explanation: The joke works as both a commentary on Chandler's shallowness and a wink to the audience about Rachel's character (famous for dating). Rewatch bonus: viewers know Ross is the father and this hits differently.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Dating is impossible when you're a single mother. I mean, what man wants to deal with that baggage?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Well, I mean, not to brag, but I've dated women with kids.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Yeah, and how'd that work out?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I'm not saying it worked out.

jokes.text: I don't know. / Are you okay? / Mm-hm. I'm just thinking about Phoebe. Poor, knocked-up Phoebe.
jokes.setup: Monica and Chandler are ostensibly discussing 'Phoebe's' pregnancy (which is actually Rachel's)
jokes.punchline: Monica's 'Poor, knocked-up Phoebe' is dripping with false sympathy — the audience knows Monica is actually thinking about Rachel and perhaps herself
jokes.explanation: The dramatic irony of Monica sympathy-performing about 'Phoebe' while actually processing Rachel's pregnancy works adequately. Not a strong standalone joke but functions as a scene beat.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Whoa, whoa, whoa! I was just... aerating the champagne. It's a very sophisticated French technique.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: You spilled it all over the carpet.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Yes, well, the carpet needed aerating too.

jokes.text: That's actually how the French drink it.
jokes.setup: Someone has apparently spilled or awkwardly consumed champagne
jokes.punchline: An offhand claim that the embarrassing way they drank is the correct French method — a classic social-save joke
jokes.explanation: Generic social-save joke that could appear in any sitcom. Low character integration, but the economy is reasonable. Functional filler.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Well, I'm not going to break up his marriage. I mean, I'm not a home-wrecker. I would just be there, you know, in case something happens. Like if Barbara dies.

jokes.text: When I got pregnant with the triplets, I took the test three times. / Maybe it's a false-positive. Are you sure you peed on the stick right? / How many ways are there to do that?
jokes.setup: Phoebe is trying to calm Rachel by suggesting the pregnancy test might be wrong
jokes.punchline: She asks 'Are you sure you peed on the stick right?' — implying Rachel may have failed at this basic task; Rachel's incredulous 'How many ways are there to do that?' is the punchline
jokes.explanation: Phoebe's oblivious question and Rachel's exasperated logic are a solid exchange. The escalation — Phoebe went from 'maybe false positive' to questioning Rachel's ability to urinate on an object — is funny.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: What? There's a technique?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Well, you have to aim.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Aim? Okay, I'm not trying to take down a duck here!

jokes.text: You gotta take it again, as a present to me.
jokes.setup: Rachel says she'll take another test at home; Phoebe insists she do it now
jokes.punchline: Phoebe frames watching Rachel take a pregnancy test as a 'present to me' — treating it as a wedding gift
jokes.explanation: Phoebe's framing of a pregnancy test as a gift is characteristically unfiltered and funny. It reframes the drama as a social transaction in classic Phoebe style.

dialogue.line: Wedding registries prevent awkward gift situations

jokes.text: Come on! It's my wedding. That could be my present. / Hey! I just gave you peeing on a stick. / See, this is why you register.
jokes.setup: Monica demands to know the father as her wedding present; Phoebe reminds her she's already given her the pregnancy test
jokes.punchline: Rachel's 'See, this is why you register' — delivered as genuine domestic wisdom — reframes the entire argument through the lens of gift registry etiquette
jokes.explanation: One of the strongest jokes in the episode. 'See, this is why you register' takes the absurd premise (pregnancy test as wedding gift), treats it with complete seriousness, and applies real-world gift-giving logic to it. The joke works on multiple levels: it's a perfect deadpan observation, it's character-specific to Rachel (fashion/lifestyle-conscious), and it's genuinely surprising. The economy is exceptional — five words do enormous work. This is the kind of joke that gets quoted for years.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: That was just... my stomach. I haven't eaten all day.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: No, seriously, it's a medical condition. Very common. Happens to lots of people.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: It's definitely not what you think it was. I'm fine. Completely fine.

jokes.text: It was the chair again, okay? I'm not doing it!
jokes.setup: An implied visual moment where Ross appears to have made a flatulent noise — or is perceived to have done so — near a table of wedding guests
jokes.punchline: His defensive 'It was the chair again, okay? I'm not doing it!' reveals this has happened before at this event — and that the chair is apparently his alibi
jokes.explanation: The 'it was the chair' implication is broad but the detail of 'again' — meaning this has happened multiple times — and his preemptive 'I'm not doing it!' make it funnier than a single incident would be.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I can teach you a special kind of dancing where you stand on my feet.

dialogue.speaker: Woman
dialogue.line: That sounds nice.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Yeah, it's called 'The Fireman Carry.' No wait, that's not it... I mean, you just stand on my feet and I lead.

jokes.text: Dr. Geller? / I wasn't farting!
jokes.setup: A little girl from the wedding approaches Ross to ask him to dance
jokes.punchline: Ross immediately assumes she's coming to accuse him of flatulence — 'I wasn't farting!' — revealing how guilty he feels about the chair incident
jokes.explanation: A masterful callback that escalates beautifully. The little girl's innocent approach triggers Ross's panic response — 'I wasn't farting!' — which is funnier than the original chair joke because (a) it confirms his guilt, (b) the contrast of a child asking an adult to dance being met with a flatulence denial is perfect, and (c) it's completely unexpected. Excellent structure and economy. One of the episode's best laugh moments.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I'm not just a soap opera actor, okay? I'm a serious actor.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: You're right. You're also just an actor.

jokes.text: In fact, why don't we try it my special way. You can dance on my feet.
jokes.setup: Ross is trying to impress Mona by being charming to the little girl who wants to dance
jokes.punchline: He invites the little girl to dance on his feet in what he clearly believes is an endearingly cute move designed to impress Mona
jokes.explanation: The setup for a physical comedy sequence; Ross using the child as a prop to look attractive to Mona is characteristically self-serving. Functions as a setup more than a standalone joke.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Oh my God, Ross, what are you doing?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: What? I'm dancing!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: That's not dancing, that's... you're just moving your feet around.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: It's called the foot dancing technique. It's very effective with women.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Oh yeah, effective at clearing the dance floor.

jokes.text: Is the pretty lady looking? / Uh-huh. / Keep dancing.
jokes.setup: Ross is dancing with the little girl on his feet, ostensibly for her enjoyment
jokes.punchline: He whispers 'Is the pretty lady looking?' — revealing this is entirely for Mona's benefit, and that he's using a child as a prop
jokes.explanation: The reveal that Ross's whole act is performance for Mona — confirmed by his whispered 'Is the pretty lady looking?' to the child — is a sharp character beat. It encapsulates his needy romanticism and self-awareness-free manipulation.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: You know, friendship is... it's the most important thing in life. These two people here, they've shown me what it means to really care about someone, to be there for them through everything. And that's beautiful, and I'm honored to be part of their journey.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Which is why I'm excited to announce that I'll be starring in a new Broadway production called 'Two Hearts, One Love' opening this fall. It's a musical about two people who find each other against all odds, and I play the lead romantic interest. We're looking for investors, so if anyone here is interested in backing a show, see me after the reception.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Anyway, to the happy couple!

jokes.text: And the world will never know.
jokes.setup: Ross has successfully used the child to impress Mona and the moment has passed
jokes.punchline: His satisfied 'And the world will never know' implies he's gotten away with something — a melodramatic self-congratulation for a transparently obvious scheme
jokes.explanation: Ross's self-satisfaction is funny because his scheme was completely transparent. 'The world will never know' is grandiose for what was basically using a child as a flirting prop. Decent button.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I don't think this is working.

dialogue.speaker: Woman
dialogue.line: Why don't we try switching positions?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: That's not going to help. You're still going to be heavy.

jokes.text: I told him all about Days of Our Lives. / No, you don't tell a Broadway guy that! / Now he thinks I'm just a soap actor.
jokes.setup: Chandler's mom says she told Dennis about Joey's work
jokes.punchline: Joey's horror at being described as 'a soap actor' to a Broadway director — despite being literally a soap actor — is funny for his obliviousness to his own career status
jokes.explanation: Joey's objection that he doesn't want to be described accurately to someone who could help his career is a good character beat. His aspirational self-image versus reality is a core source of his comedy.

jokes.text: You are a soap actor with freakishly tiny feet.
jokes.setup: Chandler's mom is defending her description of Joey to Dennis
jokes.punchline: She adds 'with freakishly tiny feet' — a callback to the shoe size revelation — delivered as if this is a neutral, factual qualifier
jokes.explanation: A quick callback that earns a good laugh by integrating two ongoing storylines (Joey's Broadway ambitions, his tiny feet) into a single devastating sentence. The deadpan delivery of 'freakishly tiny feet' as objective descriptor is funny.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: You're a great dancer, Chandler. Really, you're amazing.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Really?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: No, not at all. You dance like a giraffe.

jokes.text: Joey's wedding toast — 'Some happy memories... some sad memories... I'm sorry... and some scared memories. Whoa!'
jokes.setup: Joey is giving a toast and says he thought back over memories with Monica and Chandler, acting them out
jokes.punchline: His toast devolves into a one-man performance where he acts out unnamed memories — 'some scared memories. Whoa!' — with physical reactions to things the audience can't see
jokes.explanation: Joey's toast is a character-perfect piece: he's trying to be sincere but can't resist performing. The physical comedy of him acting out 'scared memories' at a wedding is a rewatch-bonus visual gag. His resume pitch at the end ('willing to do partial nudity') is the perfect button — he transforms the heartfelt toast into a casting call.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Hey! Those are my dance moves!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: What? You can't copyright the running man.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I've been working on my moves since high school. They're original.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Ross, everyone does the running man.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Not like this. I have a very specific rhythm and arm angle.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Maybe you should trademark them. 'The Geller Glide' or something.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh my God, that's actually not a bad idea.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Yes it is. It's the worst idea anyone's had in the history of ideas.

jokes.text: Their friend who can speak in many dialects, has training in stage combat, and is willing to do partial nudity.
jokes.setup: Joey concludes a heartfelt toast about Monica and Chandler by describing himself as their loyal friend
jokes.punchline: His description of himself — 'speaks in many dialects, stage combat, willing to do partial nudity' — is a résumé, not a character endorsement
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's standout jokes. Joey converts a wedding toast into a de facto audition by describing his friendship in actor-résumé terms. 'Willing to do partial nudity' as the final credential — the most intimate detail of an actor's casting profile being offered as friendship — is brilliantly absurd. The structure is perfect: emotional buildup, then a complete pivot to self-promotion. Very high character integration; this joke only exists because Joey is an actor whose career and identity are inseparable.

dialogue.line: False result that sets up bigger revelation

jokes.text: So what's your name? / Gert. / That's pretty.
jokes.setup: Ross is now dancing with an elderly woman who has pushed her way onto his feet
jokes.punchline: Ross says 'That's pretty' about the name Gert — a reaction that is clearly performative, as 'Gert' is objectively not a pretty name — the irony of his desperate politeness is the joke
jokes.explanation: A quick beat on Ross's compulsive need to be charming/polite. Saying 'that's pretty' about the name Gert is so transparently false that the insincerity IS the joke. Functional but not exceptional.

jokes.text: What are you doing, Gert? / Dancing on your feet like the other girls did it. / ... Okay. Hop on, Gert.
jokes.setup: An elderly woman named Gert has gotten Ross to invite her to dance on his feet; she is not being gentle
jokes.punchline: Gert aggressively stands on Ross's feet and starts demanding he go faster — reversing the power dynamic completely; Ross's resigned 'Hop on, Gert' is a defeated surrender
jokes.explanation: A strong physical escalation of the dance-on-feet gag. The little girl was charming; Gert is a chaos agent who barks orders and injures Ross. The inversion of the cute scenario into something painful and absurd is well-structured. The sequence builds to the later payoff of Ross limping.

jokes.text: Why aren't you moving your feet? / I'm trying. / Faster! You're not going fast enough! / Maybe I should stand on your feet!
jokes.setup: Gert is standing on Ross's feet demanding he dance
jokes.punchline: Ross's desperate suggestion — 'Maybe I should stand on your feet!' — as a proposed reversal reveals how much pain he's in
jokes.explanation: Good escalation beat within the Gert sequence. Ross's 'Maybe I should stand on YOUR feet' is a funny reversal proposition. The physical absurdity of a grown man being tyrannized by a small elderly woman on the dance floor is well-sustained.

dialogue.speaker: Mona
dialogue.line: Nice guys are so rare these days. I feel like I'm defending niceness single-handedly.

jokes.text: So did you happen to catch my toast up there? / Oh, my God. That was for my benefit?
jokes.setup: Joey approaches Dennis the Broadway director after his toast
jokes.punchline: Dennis's 'Oh, my God. That was for my benefit?' reveals he immediately understood the toast was a casting stunt — which makes Joey's obliviousness even funnier
jokes.explanation: Dennis's instant recognition punctures Joey's delusion. The fact that Joey was so obvious that Dennis clocked it immediately as a career pitch adds a layer of embarrassment to the comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Mona
dialogue.line: Wait, so Joey really does have unusually large feet?

jokes.text: It's an all-Chinese cast. / Can you be Chinese? / I'm not proud of this, but... / Oh, my God. No, please! Don't!
jokes.setup: Dennis tells Joey he's wrong for the part because it's an all-Chinese cast
jokes.punchline: Joey's response — 'I'm not proud of this, but...' (implying he's about to demonstrate a racist impression) — and Dennis's horrified reaction tell us everything without showing us anything
jokes.explanation: The joke works by negative space: we don't see what Joey does but Dennis's 'Oh, my God. No, please! Don't!' tells us it's deeply inappropriate. Joey's 'I'm not proud of this' acknowledges the impropriety while proceeding anyway — perfect character moment. The economy of letting the audience's imagination do the work is excellent.

jokes.text: Ready to get back on the dance floor? / Did it turn into sand?
jokes.setup: Monica tries to get Chandler back on the dance floor
jokes.punchline: Chandler's 'Did it turn into sand?' — asking if the floor has become easier to navigate — is a perfectly absurd non-sequitur that expresses his resistance through weird lateral thinking
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's sharpest lines. 'Did it turn into sand?' takes the logical shape of a reasonable question (is the slippery floor better now?) but the specific answer of 'sand' is absurdly wrong — sand would be worse. The joke works because the internal logic is perfect (soft surface = easier?) but the conclusion is bizarre. Very Chandler: deflecting with specific, weird humor. Exceptional economy.

jokes.text: For the first time, I didn't want you to be embarrassed to be seen on the dance floor with some clumsy idiot. / Aww. Sweetie, you could never embarrass me. / Okay, you could easily embarrass me. But it doesn't matter. Right? I married you.
jokes.setup: Chandler explains emotionally why he took dance lessons
jokes.punchline: Monica starts to give the conventional sitcom response ('you could never embarrass me') then immediately corrects herself: 'Okay, you could easily embarrass me. But it doesn't matter.'
jokes.explanation: Monica's self-correction is the joke — she starts with the expected romantic line and then overrides it with the truth. The pivot from conventional sentiment to brutal honesty ('you could easily embarrass me') is very Monica, and 'But it doesn't matter. I married you.' recovers the sweetness. Good structure.

jokes.text: Chandler, I'm gonna have you arrested. / Why? / You stole my moves.
jokes.setup: Chandler and Monica are now dancing well; Ross observes
jokes.punchline: Ross accuses Chandler of stealing his dance moves — the same moves that just involved standing on a small child and an aggressive elderly woman
jokes.explanation: Ross calling his foot-dancing-with-children 'moves' and threatening Chandler with arrest for copying is a funny callback. The grandiosity of 'I'm gonna have you arrested' for dance-move theft is perfectly Ross. Good economy.

jokes.text: Chandler, I'm gonna have you arrested. / Why? / You stole my moves.
jokes.setup: Chandler has apparently improved his dancing; Ross watches from the sideline
jokes.punchline: Ross accuses Chandler of stealing his dance moves — implying Ross considers his awkward moves legally protected intellectual property
jokes.explanation: The threat of arrest for move-theft is exactly the right level of absurd grievance for Ross. His sense of proprietary outrage over his dance moves, combined with 'I'm gonna have you arrested,' makes this a good Ross joke. The economy is sharp — three beats, three laughs.

jokes.text: It's time. / No! / Go ahead, Rach. / Oh, wait. You know what? I can't look at it. I can't look at it. Somebody else tell me.
jokes.setup: The pregnancy test timer is up and Rachel has to look at the result
jokes.punchline: Rachel's escalating panic — 'No!' then 'I can't look at it. I can't look at it.' — builds comedically before she delegates the reading to someone else
jokes.explanation: More of a tense dramatic beat with mild comedy than a strong joke. Rachel's refusal to look is relatable but doesn't deliver a sharp punchline. Functions as setup for the negative/positive reversal.

jokes.text: It's negative. / What? / It's negative. / (long pause) Well, there you go. / Whew! / That is... that is really great, great news.
jokes.setup: Rachel asked someone else to read the test; it comes back negative
jokes.punchline: Rachel's reaction — the long, uncomfortable pauses, the forced 'That is really great, great news' — reveals she is NOT relieved, despite saying all the right words
jokes.explanation: This is subtle comedy through performance — Rachel's stilted 'That is... that is really great, great news' and the awkward silences convey the opposite of what she's saying. It's comedic AND emotionally effective. Good structural use of the pause as comedic beat.

jokes.text: Because the whole...not being ready, the financial aspects, all that... This is so just the way it was supposed to be. Well then, great.
jokes.setup: Rachel trying to convince herself the negative result is what she wanted
jokes.punchline: Her increasingly hollow rationalizations and the gap between her words and visible emotions
jokes.explanation: The comedy here is pure cringe — Rachel's internal monologue externalizing as increasingly unconvincing self-reassurance. 'This is so just the way it was supposed to be' is the peak of her delusion, and 'Well then, great' as the flat response is perfect. The audience is laughing through the heartbreak.

jokes.text: God. This is so stupid. How can I be upset over something I never had?
jokes.setup: Rachel is visibly upset about the negative result despite having just said it was great news
jokes.punchline: Her self-aware observation — 'How can I be upset over something I never had?' — is both genuinely touching and lightly comic in its logic
jokes.explanation: More dramatic than comedic, but it functions as a bittersweet character beat that sets up the reversal. Included as a mild comedic moment of self-aware Rachel-ness.

jokes.text: It's negative? / No, it's positive. / What? / It's not negative, it's positive. / Are you sure? / Yeah, I lied before.
jokes.setup: Rachel has been grieving a negative pregnancy test; Phoebe suddenly tells her it's actually positive
jokes.punchline: Phoebe casually admits 'I lied before' — she deliberately gave Rachel the wrong result to force her to realize how she actually felt
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best structural moments — Phoebe's gambit to make Rachel discover her true feelings is both plot-significant and genuinely funny. 'I lied before' delivered casually is a great punchline. The reversal (negative → positive) has comedic and emotional power simultaneously. Rewatch bonus because knowing the deception makes the negative-reaction scene funnier.

jokes.text: Now you know how you really feel about it. / Oh! That's a risky little game.
jokes.setup: Phoebe explains her deception as an emotional manipulation technique
jokes.punchline: Rachel's 'That's a risky little game' — delivered with contained exasperation — perfectly captures the absurdity of Phoebe's well-meaning but insane intervention
jokes.explanation: Rachel's understatement of calling Phoebe's deception 'a risky little game' — when it was actually a major psychological manipulation — is a perfect comedic summary. 'Little game' especially earns the laugh because it miniaturizes something huge.

jokes.text: With who? / No, it's still not the time.
jokes.setup: Rachel has just joyfully announced she's going to have a baby
jokes.punchline: In the middle of the emotional high, Phoebe immediately asks 'With who?' — the father question returning as a running gag
jokes.explanation: A running gag payoff: Phoebe can't let the father mystery go even during Rachel's emotional revelation. The timing — immediately deflating the sentimental high with the same question — is good structural comedy.

jokes.text: With who? / No, it's still not the time.
jokes.setup: Rachel has just joyfully announced she's going to have a baby
jokes.punchline: Phoebe — in the midst of the emotional celebration — immediately asks 'With who?' and is shut down again
jokes.explanation: Perfect runner beat — in the middle of an emotionally triumphant moment, Phoebe cannot help herself and immediately loops back to the question everyone has. The timing (right after a joyful announcement) makes it land well.

jokes.text: I just didn't see the fast song coming. / Shh. Don't try to talk. We'll get you up to your room, soak your feet. You'll be okay.
jokes.setup: Ross is being helped off the dance floor, apparently injured
jokes.punchline: Monica treating Ross like a wounded soldier — 'Don't try to talk. We'll get you up to your room, soak your feet. You'll be okay' — reveals the Gert dancing sequence has caused real physical damage
jokes.explanation: A satisfying callback payoff to the Gert physical comedy. 'I just didn't see the fast song coming' is Ross's dignified attempt to explain why an elderly woman destroyed his feet. Monica's emergency-triage response ('Don't try to talk') is good escalation.

jokes.text: There's so few genuinely nice guys out there. / Tell me about it. / I feel like I'm holding down the fort all by myself. / It's Joey, right? / Yeah. / Wait a minute! No! I'm the nice one! I'm the one that danced with the kids all night!
jokes.setup: Monica compliments Joey for being sweet and genuinely nice
jokes.punchline: Ross overhears the compliment and furiously claims the title of 'the nice one' on the basis of dancing with children — not realizing this undercuts any sense of genuine niceness
jokes.explanation: A perfect ironic callback. Ross's dancing-with-children was entirely self-serving (to impress Mona), and now he invokes it as evidence of authentic niceness. His competitive indignation — 'Wait a minute! No! I'm the nice one!' — is funny, and 'holding down the fort all by myself' as Joey's self-description is also characteristically oblivious.

jokes.text: How small are your feet?
jokes.setup: Ross has just claimed being 'the nice one' on the basis of dancing with children all night; Monica has been treating his foot injuries
jokes.punchline: Monica's final line — 'How small are your feet?' — connects Ross's injured feet to the Joey shoe-size storyline as a final button, while also being a genuinely funny non-sequitur coda
jokes.explanation: A closing callback that wraps the episode. The question of Ross's foot size is both a callback to Joey's tiny feet and a final indignity for Ross. The economy — a four-word question as the episode's last joke — is very good.

tmdb_overview: The excitement of Monica and Chandler's wedding is diminished by the news that someone may be pregnant. Chandler's hopes of not embarrassing Monica on the dance floor are ruined by his slippery new shoes, and Ross' attempts to flirt with an attractive wedding guest.
insight: Post-wedding chaos yields 47 jokes, but emotional weight softens the comedy.
